questions.question: Systems are usefully divided in three by their response-time expectations. Which three?

options.text: Services, batch processing systems, and stream processing systems
OLTP, OLAP, and hybrid transactional-analytical systems
Synchronous, asynchronous, and partially synchronous systems
Leader-based, multi-leader, and leaderless systems

questions.explanation: A service waits on a user and is judged by response time; a batch job runs over bounded input and is judged by throughput; a stream processor consumes unbounded input shortly after events occur.

questions.question: What style of data processing do Parts I and II assume, and which systems work that way?

options.text: Requests and queries, with their responses or results
Batch jobs scheduled nightly, as in data warehouses
Streams of events processed continuously
Peer-to-peer gossip between nodes

questions.explanation: Request/response is so ingrained it's easy to take for granted — but it is not the only way of building systems.

questions.question: What can generally be assumed about a request in an online system?

options.text: That a human triggers it and is waiting for the response
That it is triggered by another machine and nobody is waiting
That it is idempotent and can be retried freely
That it touches only one partition

questions.explanation: A waiting human is what makes response time the governing metric.

questions.question: Match the three system types to their primary performance measure. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Services (online systems) wait for a request or instruction to arrive and try to handle it as quickly as possible, sending a response back; response time is usually the primary measure of performance, and availability is often very important — if the client can't reach the service, the user will probably get an error message

Batch processing systems (offline systems) take a large amount of input data, run a job to process it, and produce some output data; the primary performance measure is usually throughput — the time it takes to crunch through an input dataset of a certain size

Stream processing systems (near-real-time systems) consume inputs and produce outputs rather than responding to requests; a stream job operates on events shortly after they happen, which allows lower latency than the equivalent batch systems
All three of them are measured primarily by their availability rather than by throughput or latency, because a system that is reachable is by definition keeping up with its workload

questions.explanation: Response time, throughput, and latency respectively.

questions.question: How long do batch jobs take, and how are they started?

options.text: They take minutes to days, with no user waiting for the result
Jobs take seconds and are triggered by user requests
Jobs take hours and are triggered by incoming events
Jobs run continuously with no scheduling

questions.explanation: Minutes to days, on a periodic schedule, with nobody waiting.

questions.question: On what property does the line between stream and batch processing fall?

options.text: On the boundedness of the input
On latency alone, which is the defining difference
On whether the data is in HDFS or in a queue
On whether the job is scheduled or continuous

questions.explanation: Boundedness, not latency, is the structural distinction — latency is a consequence. Chapter 11 builds upon batch processing.

questions.question: When was MapReduce published, what was it called, and where was it implemented?

options.text: Published in 2004, and called the algorithm behind Google's scalability
Published in 1998, called 'the Google File System', implemented in HDFS
Published in 2008, called 'the Hadoop algorithm', implemented in Spark and Flink
Published in 2004, called 'bulk synchronous parallel', implemented in Pregel

questions.explanation: 2004, with the overenthusiastic label the chapter quotes from The Perils of JavaSchools.

questions.question: What was MapReduce's actual novelty, and why is it still worth studying?

options.text: Not novel as a programming model, but robustly scalable at Google
It was novel as a programming model and remains the state of the art
It was novel in neither respect and is no longer worth studying
It was novel in its query language, which is still widely used

questions.explanation: Scale on commodity hardware, not conceptual novelty.

questions.question: What are the historical antecedents of batch processing?

options.text: Punch card tabulating machines, as in the 1890 US Census
The ENIAC of 1945 and the IBM System/360 of 1964
Punched tape systems from the 1920s, and nothing earlier
Batch processing has no genuine pre-computer ancestor

questions.explanation: 1890 to 2004 is 114 years; the 1978 statement of the Unix philosophy to the 2004 MapReduce paper is 26 years — and the chapter says surprisingly little has changed in four decades.

questions.question: An nginx access log line reads: 216.58.210.78 - - [27/Feb/2015:17:55:11 +0000] 'GET /css/typography.css HTTP/1.1' 200 3377 'http://martin.kleppmann.com/' 'Mozilla/5.0 ... Chrome/40.0.2214.115'. What does it tell us? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That the request was made on February 27, 2015, at 17:55:11 UTC, for the file /css/typography.css, from the client IP address 216.58.210.78
That the user was not authenticated, so the remote_user field is set to a hyphen
That the response status was 200, meaning the request was successful, and the response was 3,377 bytes in size
That the browser was Chrome 40, and that the request carried no referrer header at all

questions.explanation: The log line does carry a referrer: the file was loaded because it was referenced in the page at that URL. There's a lot of information in one line — to interpret it you need to look at the definition of the log format. The example posits a web server that appends a line to a log file every time it serves a request, which makes the log append-only, immutable and bounded.

questions.question: In the Unix pipeline for finding the five most popular pages, what does 'awk {print $7}' do?

options.text: It splits each line on whitespace and prints the seventh field
It prints the seventh line of the whole input file
It prints the seventh character of every input line
It counts seven fields per line and discards the rest

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that some people love to point out that cat is unnecessary here, since the input file could be given directly as an argument to awk — but the linear pipeline is more apparent when written like this. The seventh whitespace-separated field lands on the URL because the request field is quoted and splits into three whitespace fields.

questions.question: The first sort produces no counts and no ranking. Why is it there?

options.text: Because sorting groups repeated URLs into adjacent lines
Because the head command requires its input to be sorted
Because awk emits its output fields in a random order
It is unnecessary and could be removed from the pipeline

questions.explanation: Adjacency is what makes counting possible without a hash table. This sort step is implicit in MapReduce.

questions.question: What do 'uniq -c' and 'sort -r -n' each do?

options.text: It collapses adjacent duplicate lines and -c prints the count
uniq removes duplicates without counting; sort -r -n sorts alphabetically in reverse
uniq counts all lines; sort -r -n sorts by URL numerically
uniq sorts and counts; sort -r -n reverses the file

questions.explanation: Each program does one thing well. Finally head outputs just the first five lines (-n 5) of input and discards the rest, giving the top five pages.

questions.question: The output shows 4189 /favicon.ico, 3631 for an SSH keys article, 2124 for a schema evolution article, 1369 for /, and 915 for /css/typography.css. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The top five URLs account for 12,228 requests in total
The single most-requested URL accounts for about 34% of that total
The top entry, /favicon.ico, is arguably not a 'page' at all — it is the browser's tab icon
The top five URLs between them account for about 8,000 requests

questions.question: You are asked to omit CSS files from the report, and separately to rank client IP addresses rather than pages. What changes?

options.text: Only the awk stage changes
The entire pipeline must be rewritten for each variation
The sort stage changes in the first case and head in the second
Those variations require a different toolchain, since awk cannot express either filter

questions.explanation: One stage changes; the rest of the pipeline is untouched.

questions.question: Which Unix tools are worth learning, and what can be done with them?

options.text: awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq and xargs
find, xargs and tar, citing the POSIX standard
python, perl and ruby, citing benchmark studies
hadoop, hive and pig, citing Google's paper

questions.explanation: Six tools, with a real performance claim behind them.

questions.question: A shell pipeline counts the most popular URLs in a web server log using awk '{print $7}'. An equivalent Ruby program instead reads line.split[6]. What does the Ruby version maintain, and why does the index differ?

options.text: A hash table of counters keyed by the URL; Ruby arrays are zero-indexed while awk fields start at one
A sorted array of every URL it has seen; the indices differ because the two tools read different log formats
A database connection opened per line; the indices genuinely point at two different fields of the log
No state at all between lines; the index is arbitrary and either value would have worked equally well

questions.explanation: Same field, different indexing convention — a purely syntactic difference.

questions.question: What actually differs between the pipeline and the Ruby script?

options.text: A big difference in execution flow, visible at scale
Only the syntax differs; the execution flow is identical
The Ruby version is always faster on the same input
The pipeline version is always the more readable of the two

questions.explanation: Execution flow, not syntax, is what matters at scale.

questions.question: What do the Ruby script and the Unix pipeline each keep in memory, and what decides which is better?

options.text: The Ruby script keeps a hash table in memory; Unix sorts instead
Both keep hash tables, and the difference is the hash function used
Both sort their input, and the difference is the sorting algorithm
Each of the two avoids keeping any state in memory while it runs

questions.explanation: Hash table versus sorted repetition, decided by cardinality.

questions.question: Define working set, and what memory budget suffices for most small to mid-sized websites?

options.text: The amount of memory the job needs random access to
The working set is the total input size; 1 TB is needed
The working set is the number of log lines; 1 GB per million lines is needed
The working set is the output size; no memory is needed

questions.explanation: Distinct keys, not total records, determine the working set.

questions.question: When the working set exceeds available memory, why does sorting win?

options.text: Because sorting spills sorted chunks to disk and merges them
Because sorting uses less CPU than hashing
Because sorting requires no disk at all
Because hash tables cannot be spilled to disk in any implementation

questions.explanation: The GNU Coreutils sort utility on Linux automatically handles larger-than-memory datasets by spilling to disk, and automatically parallelizes sorting across multiple CPU cores — so it easily scales to large datasets without running out of memory, and the bottleneck becomes the rate at which the input file can be read from disk.

questions.question: Who invented Unix pipes, when, and with what analogy?

options.text: Doug McIlroy, in 1964
Ken Thompson in 1970, with a plumbing analogy
Dennis Ritchie in 1978, with an assembly-line analogy
Eric Raymond in 1999, with a Lego analogy

questions.explanation: 1964 for the description, with the garden-hose image that gave pipes their name.

questions.question: Which are the four principles of the Unix philosophy as published in 1978? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new 'features'

Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program. Don't clutter output with extraneous information, avoid stringently columnar or binary input formats, and don't insist on interactive input
Design and build software, even operating systems, to be tried early, ideally within weeks. Don't hesitate to throw away the clumsy parts and rebuild them
Use unskilled help in preference to building tools, since the detour to build a tool is always wasteful in the end

questions.explanation: The principle runs the other way: use tools in preference to unskilled help to lighten a programming task, even if you have to detour to build the tools. Principles 1 and 2 are the ones the Summary carries forward into MapReduce.

questions.question: Which properties characterize the Unix philosophy in practice, and what do they resemble?

options.text: Automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration and experimentation
Reliability, scalability, maintainability, security and compliance — compared to enterprise database design
Speed, cost, simplicity, safety and portability — compared to the cloud
The five properties are unnamed

questions.explanation: A 1978 philosophy that prefigures Agile and DevOps.

questions.question: Why is sort the exemplar Unix tool here, and what is the sting in the tail?

options.text: Because it handles datasets larger than memory by spilling to disk
Because it is the fastest tool, and there is no sting
Because it is the simplest tool, and the sting is that it is slow
Because it does many things, and the sting is that it violates the philosophy

questions.explanation: A shell like bash lets us easily compose these small programs into surprisingly powerful data processing jobs, even though many of them are written by different groups of people.

questions.question: What is the uniform interface in Unix, precisely?

options.text: A file, or more precisely a file descriptor
A record, defined as a tuple of typed fields
A stream of structured objects
A pipe, which is distinct from a file

questions.explanation: A footnote gives a second example: URLs and HTTP, the foundations of the web. A URL identifies a particular resource on a website, and you can link to any URL from any other website, so users can seamlessly jump between websites by following links even though the servers may be operated by entirely unrelated organizations — a key insight in making the web the success that it is. The pre-web counter-example is bulletin board systems, each with its own phone number and baud rate configuration: to reference content on a different BBS you had to hang up, dial the other BBS, and manually find the information, since it wasn't possible to link directly to content inside another BBS.

questions.question: Which record separator do awk, sort, uniq and head all agree on, and what would arguably have been a better choice?

options.text: A list of records separated by the newline character
They agree on the tab character; the comma would have been better
They agree on 0x1E already, which is ideal
Each tool picks its own record separator, so the choice is arbitrary

questions.explanation: Record separation is standardized; record parsing is more vague — some tools assume whitespace or tab separation, others use CSV, pipe-separated or other encodings, and even something as simple as quoting has half a dozen command-line options in xargs.

questions.question: What is unsatisfying about ASCII text as a uniform interface?

options.text: That {print $7} is not very readable
It is too slow to parse
It cannot represent binary data at all
Nothing is unsatisfying: positional field references are perfectly readable

questions.explanation: Positional field references are the cost of an untyped interface.

questions.question: How rare is Unix-grade composability today?

options.text: That it is now the exception rather than the norm
It is the norm; most modern tools compose as well as Unix tools
It is universal within cloud platforms
It has improved steadily since 1978

questions.explanation: Balkanization of data is the term for the resulting state of affairs.

questions.question: What are stdin and stdout bound to by default, and what can change the wiring?

options.text: stdin from the keyboard and stdout to the screen
Each is bound to a file by default, and only a pipe can change that
Each is bound to the network by default, with files as the exception
They cannot be rebound

questions.explanation: Pipes stream through a small buffer rather than materializing intermediate state — which is exactly what MapReduce does differently.

questions.question: What are the existing names for a program not knowing where its input comes from?

options.text: Loose coupling, late binding, or inversion of control
Encapsulation, abstraction and polymorphism
Dependency injection, service location and reflection
Modularity, cohesion and coupling

questions.explanation: Three existing names for one property, from three different traditions.

questions.question: You want to add stages that translate user-agent strings into browser identifiers and IP addresses into country codes. What must your programs do, and what does sort need to know about them?

options.text: Read from stdin and write to stdout
Your program must register with sort and declare its schema
Your program must be written in C and linked against sort
Your program must implement a plugin interface

questions.explanation: Two file descriptors are the whole contract.

questions.question: What are the limits of stdin/stdout wiring? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Programs that need multiple inputs or outputs are possible but tricky
You can't pipe a program's output into a network connection

If a program directly opens files for reading and writing, or starts another program as a subprocess, or opens a network connection, then that I/O is wired up by the program itself — it can still be configurable via command-line options, but the flexibility of wiring up inputs and outputs in a shell is reduced
Unix programs are unable to read from files at all, only from standard input

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that except by using a separate tool such as netcat or curl, and that Unix started out trying to represent everything as files but the BSD sockets API deviated from that convention — the research operating systems Plan 9 and Inferno are more consistent in their use of files, representing a TCP connection as a file in /net/tcp.

questions.question: Why do Unix tools make it easy to see what is going on? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The input files to Unix commands are normally treated as immutable, so you can run the commands as often as you want, trying various command-line options, without damaging the input files
You can end the pipeline at any point, pipe the output into less, and look at it to see if it has the expected form — this ability to inspect is great for debugging
You can write the output of one pipeline stage to a file and use that file as input to the next stage, which lets you restart the later stage without rerunning the entire pipeline
They ship with a query optimizer that can explain the plan it chose

questions.explanation: So even though Unix tools are quite blunt, simple tools compared to a query optimizer of a relational database, they remain amazingly useful, especially for experimentation.

questions.question: What is the biggest limitation of Unix tools?

options.text: That they run only on a single machine
That they only handle text, not binary data
That they cannot be scripted
That they have no fault tolerance

questions.explanation: Single-machine execution is the one limitation Hadoop exists to remove.

questions.question: Complete and defend the analogy: MapReduce is a bit like Unix tools, but…

options.text: Distributed across potentially thousands of machines
…with a declarative query language instead of shell commands
…running on a single very large machine
…operating on streams rather than files

questions.explanation: A job is a process; HDFS is the filesystem.

questions.question: What two Unix-like restraints does a MapReduce job observe?

options.text: It does not modify its input and has no side effects
It modifies the input in place and appends to existing outputs
It may have arbitrary side effects but must not modify the input
It may modify the input but must have no side effects

questions.explanation: Immutable input, write-once output.

questions.question: What do MapReduce jobs use instead of stdin and stdout, and what is Hadoop's implementation?

options.text: HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System
They use TCP sockets; the implementation is YARN
They use local disks; the implementation is ext4
They use a message queue; the implementation is Kafka

questions.explanation: Files and pipes are substituted by a distributed filesystem — the key structural claim.

questions.question: Which storage systems are alternatives to a distributed filesystem? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Other distributed filesystems besides HDFS, such as GlusterFS and the Quantcast File System (QFS)
Object storage services such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage and OpenStack Swift, which are similar in many ways
Any of these can serve as the storage layer for a batch job, since the same distributed-filesystem principles apply
Relational databases such as PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle, which reach petabyte scale by adding read replicas

questions.explanation: A footnote names one real difference: with HDFS, computing tasks can be scheduled to run on the machine that stores a copy of a particular file, whereas object stores usually keep storage and computation separate. Reading from a local disk has a performance advantage if network bandwidth is a bottleneck — but note that if erasure coding is used, the locality advantage is lost, because the data from several machines must be combined in order to reconstitute the original file.

questions.question: Which principle is HDFS based on, and what does it contrast with?

options.text: The shared-nothing principle
The shared-disk principle, in contrast to shared-nothing
The shared-memory principle, in contrast to message passing
The shared-everything principle, in contrast to partitioning

questions.explanation: Commodity hardware on a conventional network is the whole point.

questions.question: How is HDFS put together?

options.text: A daemon on each machine exposing a network file service
It consists of a single storage server with attached disks
It consists of daemons only, with no central metadata server
It consists of a NameNode only, with data stored in S3

questions.explanation: Per-machine daemons plus a central block map.

questions.question: How does HDFS survive machine and disk failure?

options.text: Replicated across several machines, or erasure-coded
It relies on RAID within each individual machine only
It relies on nightly backups written out to tape
It does not tolerate disk failure at all by design

questions.explanation: At the time of writing, the biggest HDFS deployments run on tens of thousands of machines with combined storage capacity of hundreds of petabytes — viable because the cost of data storage and access on HDFS, using commodity hardware and open source software, is much lower than that of the equivalent capacity on a dedicated storage appliance.

questions.question: State MapReduce's four-step pattern and its log-analysis counterparts. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Read a set of input files and break it up into records — in the web server log example, each record is one line in the log, so the newline is the record separator
Call the mapper function to extract a key and value from each input record — here the mapper function is awk {print $7}: it extracts the URL as the key and leaves the value empty
Sort all of the key-value pairs by key — in the log example this is done by the first sort command
Call the reducer to iterate over the sorted key-value pairs — in the log example this is implemented by the second sort command in the pipeline

questions.explanation: The reducer in the log example is uniq -c, which collapses adjacent duplicates and counts them; the second sort is a separate ordering step. Four steps, mapping exactly onto the four pipeline stages.

questions.question: Of the four steps, which do you write and which does the framework supply?

options.text: Steps 2 and 4 — the map and reduce functions
You write all four steps
You write only step 3; the framework supplies the rest
The framework supplies all four steps

questions.explanation: This is why the chapter calls MapReduce a quirky implementation of a Unix process which happens to always run the sort utility between the map phase and the reduce phase — unconditionally, whereas dataflow engines later make sorting opt-in, needed only where it is actually required.

questions.question: State the mapper's contract in full.

options.text: Once per input record, to extract a key and a value
It is called once per file and maintains state across records
It must generate exactly one key-value pair per record
It is called once per key and receives all matching records

questions.explanation: Statelessness per record is what makes mappers freely parallelizable.

questions.question: State the reducer's contract.

options.text: It collects all values for one key and calls the reducer on them
It receives one key-value pair at a time with no grouping
It receives a fully materialized list of all values for a key
It receives the entire dataset and must group it itself

questions.explanation: An iterator rather than a list is what lets a key's value set exceed memory.

questions.question: The log pipeline had a second sort. How do you get that in MapReduce?

options.text: By chaining a second job onto the first job's output
By calling sort from inside the reducer function itself
By configuring the framework to perform the sort twice
A second sort is not possible within MapReduce at all

questions.explanation: One sort per job, so a second sort means a second job.

questions.question: What does MapReduce add over a Unix pipeline, and what makes it possible?

options.text: That it parallelizes across machines without explicit parallel code
It adds a declarative query language over the input files
It adds transactions spanning several machines
It adds low-latency responses to interactive queries

questions.explanation: This is the Unix separation of logic and wiring, applied across a cluster.

questions.question: What are mappers and reducers actually written in?

options.text: Usually as functions in a conventional programming language
Only standard Unix tools may be used as mappers
Only SQL may be used to express the computation
Only C++ may be used, as is the case at Google

questions.explanation: The chapter cites Manta: Unix Meets Map Reduce for the shell-tool approach.

questions.question: What determines the map-side parallelism, and what does the scheduler try to do?

options.text: A directory in HDFS, with each file block as a partition
You choose the number of mappers, and the scheduler places them randomly
The number of mappers equals the number of machines, and data is copied to them
One mapper per input record, placed by hash

questions.explanation: In most cases the application code that should run in the map task is not yet present on the machine assigned the job, so the MapReduce framework first copies the code — for example JAR files in the case of a Java program — to the appropriate machines. It then starts the map task and begins reading the input file, passing one record at a time to the mapper callback, whose output consists of key-value pairs.

questions.question: Contrast how the numbers of map and reduce tasks are determined, and how a key reaches a reducer.

options.text: Map tasks by the input blocks; reduce tasks by configuration
Both counts are set explicitly in the job configuration
Both counts are determined by the number of input blocks
Keys reach reducers by range partitioning rather than hashing

questions.explanation: Blocks determine mappers; the author determines reducers; hashing routes keys.

questions.question: Why does the sort happen in stages, and where does mapper output go?

options.text: Because the dataset is too large to sort on one machine
Mapper output goes straight to HDFS, sorted globally in one pass
Mapper output is kept entirely in memory
Mapper output is sorted by the reducers, not the mappers

questions.explanation: Per-mapper sorted partitions on local disk, merged later by reducers.

questions.question: Define the shuffle, and what is misleading about the name?

options.text: The scheduler notifies reducers to start fetching output files
The shuffle is the random reassignment of keys to reducers; the name is apt
The shuffle is the sorting step only; the name is apt
The shuffle is the reduce phase itself, and nothing about the name is misleading

questions.explanation: Partition, sort and copy — deterministic throughout, despite the name.

questions.question: Describe the reduce side from fetched files to written output.

options.text: It merges the mapper files together, preserving the sort order
The reducer sorts the fetched files itself before processing
The reducer writes output to its local disk only, with no replication
The reducer receives unsorted records and must group them in memory

questions.explanation: Merge preserving order, then one reducer call per key.

questions.question: Why is a single MapReduce job usually not enough, and how are jobs chained?

options.text: That a single job can answer only limited questions
Jobs are chained by an explicit workflow API in Hadoop MapReduce
Jobs are chained through in-memory pipes
Jobs cannot be chained

questions.explanation: Directory names are the entire chaining mechanism — chained jobs are less like pipelines of Unix commands, which pass output as input directly using only a small in-memory buffer, and more like a sequence of commands where each command's output is written to a temporary file and the next command reads from that file.

questions.question: When is a batch job's output valid, and who enforces workflow dependencies?

options.text: Only when the job completes successfully
Partial output is valid; jobs may start as soon as any input appears
The MapReduce framework enforces dependencies internally
HDFS enforces dependencies through file locks

questions.explanation: All-or-nothing output, with an external scheduler enforcing ordering.

questions.question: How big do workflows get, and which higher-level tools wire them automatically?

options.text: Fifty to a hundred MapReduce jobs
Workflows rarely exceed 5 jobs; no tooling is needed
Workflows reach thousands of jobs; only Oozie can manage them
Workflows are always single jobs in practice

questions.explanation: 50 to 100 jobs, with cross-team dependencies — hence the tooling.

questions.question: When is a join necessary, and what does denormalization do about it?

options.text: A foreign key, a document reference, or a graph edge
A join is necessary only in relational models; denormalization removes it entirely
A join is never necessary in batch processing
Joins matter only for graph-shaped data, so denormalization is beside the point

questions.explanation: A footnote restricts the chapter's discussion to equi-joins, the most common type of join in which a record is associated with other records that have an identical value in a particular field — some databases support more general types of joins, for example using a less-than operator instead of an equality operator.

questions.question: What does MapReduce do instead of using indexes, and when is that reasonable?

options.text: It reads the entire contents of all its input files
MapReduce builds indexes on the fly for each join
MapReduce uses HDFS indexes, which are always faster than scans
MapReduce refuses joins entirely

questions.explanation: In a batch context, join means resolving all occurrences of some association within a dataset — the data for all users simultaneously, not merely looking up the data for one particular user, which would be done far more efficiently with an index.

questions.question: A log of user activity events is joined with a database of user profiles. Describe the two datasets, and how does the join map onto a star schema?

options.text: A log of activity events, also called clickstream data
Two fact tables joined on a timestamp
Two dimension tables joined on a surrogate key
A single denormalized table requiring no join

questions.explanation: Fact table plus dimension, joined on user ID.

questions.question: Why would querying the user database for every event perform poorly? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The processing throughput would be limited by the round-trip time to the database server
The effectiveness of a local cache would depend very much on the distribution of data
Running a large number of queries in parallel could easily overwhelm the database
The database would refuse to accept that many concurrent connections

questions.explanation: It is possible, but it would most likely suffer from very poor performance. Two rules follow: in order to achieve good throughput in a batch process, the computation must be local to one machine as much as possible — making random-access requests over the network for every record you want to process is too slow. And querying a remote database would mean the batch job becomes nondeterministic, because the data in the remote database might change.

questions.question: What is the better approach to the join, and where does the copy go?

options.text: Put a copy of the user database in the distributed filesystem
Query the live database from the reducer rather than the mapper
Replicate the activity log into the database
Cache the user database in each mapper's memory from the network

questions.explanation: Both sides in HDFS, joined by the framework.

questions.question: In the reduce-side sort-merge join, what does each set of mappers emit?

options.text: Two sets of mappers, both keyed by user ID
Both sets emit the event timestamp as the key
Only the activity mappers emit; the user database is loaded into memory
Both sets emit the date of birth as the key

questions.explanation: Same key from both sides is what brings the records together.

questions.question: Name and define the technique that guarantees the reducer sees the user record first.

options.text: Secondary sort, so the database record arrives first
Primary sort, which orders by key only
Total order partitioning, which orders reducers
Combiner ordering, which pre-aggregates on the map side

questions.explanation: Secondary sort orders the values within a key, not just the keys.

questions.question: Walk the reducer's join logic and its output.

options.text: Once per user ID, with the date of birth arriving first
The reducer is called once per activity event and queries the user database
The reducer buffers all records for all users in memory
The reducer emits the raw records unchanged

questions.explanation: Because the reducer processes all of the records for a particular user ID in one go, it only needs to keep one user record in memory at any one time and never needs to make any requests over the network. This algorithm is known as a sort-merge join, since mapper output is sorted by key and the reducers then merge together the sorted lists of records from both sides of the join — a fairly simple, single-threaded piece of code that can churn through records with high throughput and low memory overhead.

questions.question: Explain the 'mappers send messages to the reducers' metaphor.

options.text: The mappers as senders and the reducers as recipients
The key is literally an IP address and port
The mappers open TCP connections to the reducers directly
The metaphor applies only to Pregel, not to MapReduce

questions.explanation: An address-like key, without being a network address.

questions.question: What two aspects does MapReduce separate, and what extra protection does that buy?

options.text: It separates the network communication from the application logic
It separates reads from writes, which buys durability
It separates storage from compute, which buys elasticity
It separates mappers from reducers, which buys nothing extra

questions.explanation: Communication separated from logic, with transparent retries as a bonus.

questions.question: What is the second common use of the 'bring related data together' pattern, and how is it implemented?

options.text: Grouping records by some key, as SQL's GROUP BY does
Filtering records, implemented in the reducer
Sorting records, implemented by the framework alone
Deduplicating records, implemented by a combiner

questions.explanation: Grouping and joining are structurally the same operation in MapReduce.

questions.question: Define sessionization and its business uses.

options.text: Collating all activity events for one user session
Splitting one user's events across many servers for load balancing
Counting total page views per day
Deduplicating events by timestamp

questions.explanation: Multiple web servers scattering one user's events is what makes the grouping necessary.

questions.question: What breaks the 'bring all records with the same key to the same place' pattern, and what are its names?

options.text: A very large amount of data for a single key
Too many distinct keys, known as fan-out
Too few reducers, known as underpartitioning
Unsorted input, known as disorder

questions.explanation: One slow reducer stalls the whole workflow.

questions.question: Describe the skewed join method in Pig.

options.text: It samples first to find hot keys, then spreads them over reducers
It routes all of the hot-key records to a single dedicated reducer
It drops the hot-key records and processes them in a later pass
It hashes the hot keys twice in order to spread them further

questions.explanation: Very similar to the technique of using randomization to alleviate hot spots in a partitioned database.

questions.question: Match the three tools to their skew-handling methods.

options.text: Pig samples first; Crunch requires the hot keys to be named
All three use sampling jobs and random reducer assignment
All three require explicit hot-key specification
Pig requires explicit keys; Crunch and Hive use sampling

questions.explanation: Sampling in Pig, explicit specification in Crunch and Hive.

questions.question: For grouping and aggregating by a hot key, which two-stage technique works?

options.text: A first stage groups a random subset, and a second combines them
A single stage configured with a larger number of reducers
A first stage that drops hot keys and a second that reprocesses them
Two stages which each aggregate the full dataset independently

questions.explanation: Partial aggregation shrinks the data before the final combine.

questions.question: Why are these called reduce-side joins, and what are the advantage and disadvantage?

options.text: Because the join logic runs in the reducers
Because the join happens in the mappers; the advantage is speed
Because the reducers sort; the advantage is that no assumptions are needed and there is no cost
Because HDFS performs the join; the disadvantage is network load

questions.explanation: Generality bought with shuffle cost.

questions.question: What assumption unlocks a map-side join, and what does the job look like?

options.text: A map-side join, with no reducers and no sorting
It requires more reducers and extra sorting
It requires the input to be unsorted and unpartitioned
It requires a second job to merge results

questions.explanation: No reducers, no sorting — mappers read blocks and write output.

questions.question: State the precondition and algorithm for a broadcast hash join, and explain both halves of the name.

options.text: A large dataset joined with one small enough to fit in memory
Both inputs must be small; the name refers to broadcasting to reducers
The small input is partitioned; the name refers to a hash partitioner
The large input is loaded into memory; the name is arbitrary

questions.explanation: This join method is supported by Pig under the name replicated join, by Hive as MapJoin, and by Cascading and Crunch; it is also used in data warehouse query engines such as Impala. A footnote notes the description assumes exactly one entry for each key in the hash table, probably true with a user database since a user ID uniquely identifies a user — in general the hash table may need several entries with the same key, and the join operator will output all matches for a key.

questions.question: What is the alternative to an in-memory hash table for the small join input?

options.text: Keep the small input in a read-only index on local disk
Store it in a remote database and query that once per record
Store it in HDFS and read it back once per input record
Loading it fully into memory is the only workable option here

questions.explanation: The page cache does the caching for you, lifting the memory constraint.

questions.question: Describe the partitioned hash join for those two datasets.

options.text: If both inputs are partitioned the same way
All mappers load the whole user database, as in a broadcast join
Each mapper reads all partitions of both datasets
The partitions must differ between the two sides

questions.explanation: Ten partitions means each hash table is one tenth the size.

questions.question: Under what conditions does a partitioned hash join work, and what does Hive call it?

options.text: Both inputs must have the same number of partitions
It works if either input is partitioned; Hive calls it a MapJoin
It works if both are sorted but not partitioned; Hive calls it a merge join
It works unconditionally; Hive calls it a skewed join

questions.explanation: Same count, same key, same hash function — all three required.

questions.question: What extra precondition does a map-side merge join need, and why might you run it as a separate job?

options.text: Both inputs must be partitioned and sorted on the same key
The inputs must be small enough to fit in memory
The inputs must be unsorted, since the mapper sorts them
The inputs must be in the same file

questions.explanation: No hash table is needed at all — it's a streaming merge.

questions.question: How does the choice of join affect the output layout, and where does the needed metadata live?

options.text: Reduce-side output is sorted by join key; map-side inherits the large input's layout
Both joins produce output sorted by the join key; metadata lives in HDFS block headers
Output layout is unaffected by either kind of join, so the metadata is unnecessary
Map-side joins produce unsorted output; metadata lives in ZooKeeper

questions.explanation: The output layout is inherited from the side that drives the mappers.

questions.question: Where does batch processing sit relative to OLTP and analytics?

options.text: OLTP looks up a few records by key; analytics scans in bulk
Batch processing is really a form of transaction processing
Batch processing is identical to analytics in every respect
Batch processing always produces human-readable reports

questions.explanation: Analytics-shaped access, but a different kind of output.

questions.question: What was MapReduce originally built for at Google, and how many jobs did it take?

options.text: Building the search index for Google's search engine
Building the web crawl itself, in 50 to 100 jobs
Computing PageRank scores, in one single job
Serving live search queries, in 5 to 10 jobs

questions.explanation: Note the contrast in scale: 5 to 10 jobs for search indexing versus 50 to 100 for recommendation systems.

questions.question: How does a batch process build a search index, and why are the outputs immutable?

options.text: A batch process is a very effective way to build the index
The mappers build the index and the reducers query it; outputs are mutable
A single reducer builds a global index; outputs are mutable
Indexes are built at query time, so there are no output files

questions.explanation: A Lucene-style full-text index is a file — the term dictionary — in which you can efficiently look up a particular keyword and find the list of all the document IDs containing that keyword, the postings list. A real index needs various additional data to rank search results by relevance, correct misspellings and resolve synonyms.

questions.question: Contrast the two ways to keep an index up to date.

options.text: Full rebuild of the whole index, periodically rerun
Full rebuild is cheap and incremental is expensive
Only incremental indexing is possible
Only full rebuilds are possible

questions.explanation: Simplicity versus efficiency, with segment merging as the incremental mechanism.

questions.question: Which machine learning outputs come out of batch jobs, and what problem do they create?

options.text: Classifiers and recommendation systems
Only classifiers; the output is always a report
Only recommendation systems; the output stays in HDFS
Neither: batch jobs can only build search indexes, not machine learning models

questions.explanation: Two families, both producing databases that must be served from outside Hadoop.

questions.question: Why is writing to the database from inside a mapper or reducer a bad idea? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Making a network request for every single record is orders of magnitude slower than the normal throughput of a batch task, and even if the client library supports batching, performance is likely to be poor

MapReduce jobs often run many tasks in parallel, so if all the mappers or reducers concurrently write to the same output database, that database can easily be overwhelmed — which can in turn cause operational problems in other parts of the system

Writing to an external system from inside a job produces externally visible side effects that cannot be hidden, so you have to worry about the results from partially completed jobs being visible to other systems, especially given Hadoop task attempts and speculative execution
A database is unable to accept writes from more than one client at a time

questions.explanation: The chapter also notes in passing that this only works at all if firewall rules allow direct access from your Hadoop environment to your production databases.

questions.question: State MapReduce's all-or-nothing guarantee.

options.text: A clean all-or-nothing guarantee on job output
Partial output is visible during execution and cleaned up afterward
Every task's output is visible, including retries
The guarantee applies only to reducers, not mappers

questions.explanation: Exactly-once effect from at-least-once execution, achieved by discarding losers.

questions.question: What is the right way to ship batch output into a serving database?

options.text: Build a new database inside the job and write it out as files
Write directly to the production database from the reducer, in batches
Export to CSV and import manually
Stream the output through a message queue into the database

questions.explanation: When loading data into Voldemort, the server continues serving requests to the old data files while the new data files are copied from the distributed filesystem to the server's local disk; once copying is complete, the server atomically switches over to querying the new files. If anything goes wrong it can easily switch back to the old files again, since they are still there and immutable.

questions.question: State the discipline that MapReduce inherits from Unix about how a job treats its input and its output, and the maintainability benefits that follow. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A program reads its input and writes its output; in the process, the input is left unchanged, any previous output is completely replaced with the new output, and there are no other side effects. This means you can rerun a command as often as you like, tweaking or debugging it, without messing up the state of your system

If you introduce a bug into the code and the output is wrong or corrupted, you can simply roll back to a previous version of the code and rerun the job, and the output will be correct again — or even more simply, keep the old output in a different directory and switch back to it. Databases with read-write transactions do not have this property: if you deploy buggy code that writes bad data to the database, rolling back the code will do nothing to fix the data. This ability to recover from buggy code has been called human fault tolerance

As a consequence of this ease of rolling back, feature development can proceed more quickly than in an environment where mistakes could mean irreversible damage — this principle of minimizing irreversibility is beneficial for Agile software development
If a map or reduce task fails, the framework leaves its partial output in place so that the next attempt can reuse the work already done

questions.explanation: Partial output of a failed task is discarded, precisely so that the retry is invisible — the framework reschedules the task and runs it again. Also on the list: the same set of files can be used as input for various different jobs, including monitoring jobs that calculate metrics and evaluate whether a job's output has the expected characteristics — for example by comparing it to the output from the previous run and measuring discrepancies.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Unix and Hadoop here, and how does Hadoop resolve it?

options.text: That logic is separated from wiring
Hadoop uses text files and Unix uses structured formats
The two are alike in this respect, since both of them pass around untyped text records
Hadoop eliminates the need for any interface

questions.explanation: Avro and Parquet remove the parsing tax that {print $7} represents.

questions.question: Why was the MapReduce paper 'not at all new'?

options.text: Because those algorithms already existed in MPP databases
Because MapReduce was copied from Hadoop
Because MapReduce was described in the 1978 Unix paper
Because MPP databases postdate MapReduce

questions.explanation: Generality is the difference, not the algorithms.

questions.question: What does a database require of your data that a distributed filesystem does not?

options.text: Because a distributed filesystem accepts bytes in any format
Databases require sorted input; filesystems do not
Databases require immutable data; filesystems allow mutation
The requirements the two place on incoming data are identical

questions.explanation: Hadoop opened up the possibility of indiscriminately dumping data into HDFS and only later figuring out how to process it further, whereas MPP databases typically require careful up-front modeling of the data and query patterns before importing the data into the database's proprietary storage format. From a purist's point of view careful modeling and import is desirable because users have better-quality data to work with — but in practice, simply making data available quickly, even in a quirky, difficult-to-use, raw format, is often more valuable than trying to decide on the ideal data model up front.

questions.question: Which named ideas describe raw-first data collection? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Data lake or enterprise data hub: bringing data from various parts of a large organization together in one place is valuable, because it enables joins across datasets that were previously disparate — and the careful schema design required by an MPP database slows down that centralized data collection, so collecting data in its raw form and worrying about schema design later speeds it up

Schema-on-read: indiscriminate data dumping shifts the burden of interpreting the data from the producer to the consumer, which can be an advantage if the producer and consumers are different teams with different priorities — and there may not even be one ideal data model, but rather different views onto the data that are suitable for different purposes
The sushi principle: 'raw data is better'
The waterfall principle: design the schema completely before any data is loaded, so that every consumer afterwards reads the data through one agreed model

questions.explanation: Three names for the same raw-first discipline.

questions.question: Describe the ETL pattern that Hadoop is often used for alongside an MPP data warehouse.

options.text: Raw dumps first, with interpretation deferred to the reader
Hadoop replaces the warehouse entirely, so no ETL is needed
The warehouse performs the ETL and Hadoop stores the results
ETL is performed by the transaction processing systems themselves

questions.explanation: So Hadoop and the MPP warehouse are complements, not only competitors.

questions.question: What does 'monolithic' buy an MPP database?

options.text: Monolithic and tightly integrated, tuned for one kind of query
Monolithic design buys flexibility at the cost of performance
Monolithic design buys nothing; it is purely a liability
Monolithic design buys arbitrary code execution

questions.explanation: Tight integration buys tuned performance and analyst-accessible SQL.

questions.question: Which workloads need a more general model than SQL, and why code rather than queries?

options.text: Because not all processing can be expressed as SQL queries
Only reporting workloads need code; everything else fits SQL
SQL can express all these workloads without extension
These workloads require specialized hardware, not code

questions.explanation: Application-specific logic is what resists a declarative query language.

questions.question: MPP-style SQL and MapReduce were the two processing models first available on Hadoop. Why were two models not enough?

options.text: Because MapReduce was too limiting and slow for some workloads
Because SQL was too slow and MapReduce too fast
Because two models are always sufficient; no third processing model was ever needed
Because MPP databases already offered every model

questions.explanation: Platform openness is what let the ecosystem proliferate.

questions.question: What is the single shared-use cluster argument, and which two Hadoop-ecosystem systems illustrate it?

options.text: They all run on one shared cluster over the same files
Each processing model requires its own cluster; HBase and Impala have separate storage
Only MapReduce-based systems can share a cluster
The shared cluster argument applies only to storage, not processing

questions.explanation: Shared HDFS, divergent engines.

questions.question: Which two further design differences separate MPP databases from MapReduce?

options.text: Fault handling, and the use of memory versus disk
The choice of query language and the storage format
The network topology and the scheduling policy
The isolation level and the replication factor

questions.explanation: MPP queries normally run for a few seconds or a few minutes at most, so the cost of retrying the entire query is not too great — whereas MapReduce jobs process so much data and run for so long that they are likely to experience at least one task failure along the way.

questions.question: Describe the environment MapReduce was designed for.

options.text: Mixed-use datacenters, where batch jobs can be preempted
Dedicated batch-only clusters with no priority system at all
Rented cloud virtual machines, which are never preempted
Supercomputers, which checkpoint rather than being preempted

questions.explanation: The chapter asks how realistic the fault assumptions are: in most clusters machine failures do occur but are not very frequent — probably rare enough that most jobs will not experience a machine failure — so is it really worth incurring significant overheads for the sake of fault tolerance? The answer is that preemption, not hardware failure, is the dominant cause of termination.

questions.question: Give Google's preemption figures and the 100-task claim.

options.text: About a 5% risk of being terminated within an hour
A 50% risk per hour, giving near-certain termination for 100 tasks
A 0.5% risk per hour, giving a 5% risk for 100 tasks
A 5% risk per day, giving a 50% risk for 1,000 tasks

questions.explanation: A 10-minute task is one sixth of an hour, giving roughly a 0.85% chance of being killed per task, so the chance that at least one of 100 survives-free is about 0.9915 to the hundredth power, leaving roughly a 57% chance of at least one kill — consistent with the chapter's 'greater than 50%'.

questions.question: What is the real reason MapReduce tolerates frequent termination, and who else preempts?

options.text: Because preemption is routine in a mixed-use cluster
Because commodity hardware fails constantly; all open source schedulers preempt
Because networks are unreliable; only Mesos preempts
Because disks wear out; Kubernetes preempts by default

questions.explanation: Utilization, not unreliability, is the design driver.

questions.question: Why does MapReduce deserve this much attention, and in what sense is it 'simple'?

options.text: One among many possible programming models
Because MapReduce is easy to use and remains the fastest option
Because MapReduce is the only available model
Because MapReduce is simple in both senses of the word

questions.explanation: Understandable, not easy — a distinction worth keeping straight.

questions.question: What did the higher-level programming models fix, and what could they not fix?

options.text: Pig, Hive, Cascading and Crunch
They fixed the execution model and left the API unchanged
They fixed both the API and the execution model
They fixed nothing

questions.explanation: Abstraction cannot fix an execution model. On the one hand MapReduce is very robust: you can use it to process almost arbitrarily large quantities of data on an unreliable multi-tenant system with frequent task terminations, and it will still get the job done, albeit slowly. On the other hand, other tools are sometimes orders of magnitude faster for some kinds of processing.

questions.question: Define materialization and contrast it with what Unix pipes do.

options.text: Materialization — eagerly computing and writing intermediate state
Materialization means computing on demand; pipes materialize fully
Both materialize fully; the difference is the storage medium
Each of the two streams its results, so neither materializes anything

questions.explanation: A dataset is intermediate state rather than a published dataset when the output of one job is only ever used as input to one other job maintained by the same team — and in a workflow of 50 or 100 MapReduce jobs there is a lot of such intermediate state. By contrast, if the output from the first job is a dataset you want to publish widely within your organization, other teams can refer to it by name and reuse it as input to several different jobs, and publishing data to a well-known location in the distributed filesystem allows loose coupling so that jobs don't need to know who is producing their input or consuming their output.

questions.question: What are the downsides of MapReduce's full materialization? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: No overlap between stages: a MapReduce job can only start when all tasks in the preceding jobs that generate its inputs have completed, whereas processes connected by a Unix pipe are started at the same time with output being consumed as soon as it is produced. Skew or varying load on different machines means a job often has a few straggler tasks that take much longer than the others, and having to wait for all of the preceding job's tasks slows down the execution of the workflow as a whole

Redundant mappers: mappers are often redundant, just reading back the same file that was just written by a reducer and preparing it for the next stage of partitioning and sorting — in many cases the mapper code could be part of the previous reducer, so if the reducer output was partitioned and sorted in the same way as mapper output, then reducers could be chained together directly without interleaving with mapper stages
Over-replication of temporary data: storing intermediate state in a distributed filesystem means those files are replicated across several nodes, which is often overkill for such temporary data
Loss of fault tolerance, because a materialized intermediate file cannot be re-read after a crash

questions.explanation: Materialized files are precisely what makes MapReduce's fault tolerance easy — the trade-off runs the other way.

questions.question: Name the three best-known dataflow engines and what they share.

options.text: Spark, Tez and Flink
Hive, Pig and Cascading, which share a declarative API
HBase, Impala and Drill, which share HDFS storage
Oozie, Azkaban and Airflow, which share a scheduler

questions.explanation: This style of processing engine is based on research systems like Dryad and Nephele.

questions.question: Define operator, and give the three ways a dataflow engine can wire one operator's output to another's input. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Unlike in MapReduce, these functions need not take the strict roles of alternating map and reduce, but instead can be assembled in more flexible ways — these functions are called operators
One option is to repartition and sort records by key, like the shuffle stage of MapReduce, which enables sort-merge joins and grouping in the same way as in MapReduce

Another option is to take several inputs and partition them in the same way but skip the sorting — saving effort on partitioned hash joins, where the partitioning of records is important but the order is irrelevant because building the hash table randomizes the order anyway
For broadcast hash joins, the same output from one operator is sent to just one partition of the join operator, chosen by hashing the key

questions.explanation: A broadcast hash join sends the same output to all partitions of the join operator — that is what makes it a broadcast. Sorting becomes opt-in per connection rather than unconditional.

questions.question: Which advantages do dataflow engines have over MapReduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Expensive work such as sorting need only be performed in places where it is actually required, rather than always happening by default between every map and reduce stage; and there are no unnecessary map tasks, since the work done by a mapper can often be incorporated into the preceding reduce operator because a mapper does not change the partitioning of a dataset

Because all joins and data dependencies in a workflow are explicitly declared, the scheduler has an overview of what data is required where, so it can make locality optimizations — for example placing the task that consumes some data on the same machine as the task that produces it, so the data can be exchanged through a shared memory buffer rather than having to copy it over the network

It is usually sufficient for intermediate state between operators to be kept in memory or written to local disk, which requires less I/O than writing it to HDFS where it must be replicated to several machines and written to disk on each replica — and MapReduce already uses this optimization for mapper output, but dataflow engines generalize the idea to all intermediate state
Operators must wait for the entire preceding stage to complete before any of them is allowed to begin executing

questions.explanation: That is MapReduce's behaviour, not a dataflow engine's. In a dataflow engine an operator starts as soon as its input is ready. Six advantages. You can use dataflow engines to implement the same computations as MapReduce workflows and they usually execute significantly faster — and since operators are a generalization of map and reduce, the same processing code can run on either execution engine: workflows implemented in Pig, Hive or Cascading can be switched from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with a simple configuration change, without modifying code.

questions.question: Contrast Tez with Spark and Flink as pieces of software.

options.text: Tez is thin and uses YARN's shuffle service; Spark has its own
Tez is the largest framework; Spark and Flink are thin libraries
All three are thin libraries over YARN
All three ship their own scheduler and network layer

questions.explanation: Tez borrows; Spark and Flink ship their own.

questions.question: How do Spark, Flink and Tez tolerate faults without materializing to HDFS?

options.text: That it is durable, which makes fault tolerance simple
They replicate intermediate state to three machines, like HDFS
They restart the whole job on any failure
They do not tolerate faults

questions.explanation: Lineage in Spark, operator checkpoints in Flink.

questions.question: Why does determinism matter when recomputing, and how does nondeterminism creep in? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The question matters if some of the lost data has already been sent to downstream operators: if the operator is restarted and the recomputed data is not the same as the original lost data, it becomes very hard for downstream operators to resolve the contradictions between the old and new data — so the remedy for nondeterministic operators is normally to kill the downstream operators as well and run them again on the new data. In order to avoid such cascading faults, it is better to make operators deterministic
Many programming languages do not guarantee any particular order when iterating over elements of a hash table
Many probabilistic and statistical algorithms explicitly rely on using random numbers
Any use of the system clock is deterministic, since every node in the cluster reads the same wall-clock value

questions.explanation: Clock reads and external data sources are nondeterministic, and such causes need to be eliminated before recomputation is safe. Recovering by recomputing data is not always the right answer: if the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or if the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is probably cheaper to materialize the intermediate data to files than to recompute it.

questions.question: Restate the Unix analogy for materialization, and name the one operator that cannot be pipelined.

options.text: MapReduce writes temporary files; dataflow engines are like pipes
Filtering is the blocking operator; sorting can be pipelined
Joining is the blocking operator; sorting can be pipelined
Operators in a dataflow engine never block, which is the key difference from MapReduce

questions.explanation: Sorting is inherently blocking. When the job completes its output needs to go somewhere durable so that users can find it and use it — most likely written to the distributed filesystem again. So with a dataflow engine, materialized datasets on HDFS are still usually the inputs and the final outputs of a job: like with MapReduce the inputs are immutable and the output is completely replaced, and the improvement is that you save writing all the intermediate state to the filesystem. Pipes in the middle, files at the edges.

questions.question: How does whole-graph batch processing differ from OLTP-style graph traversal queries, and what does PageRank compute?

options.text: Batch jobs run algorithms over the whole graph rather than OLTP-style traversals; PageRank ranks a page by what links to it
Batch jobs look up single vertices quickly while OLTP traversals analyse whole graphs; PageRank ranks pages by their size
They are the same use case at two different scales; PageRank simply counts the edges leaving each vertex in the graph
Both walk a few edges out from a chosen starting vertex; PageRank ranks users by how much activity they generate

questions.explanation: Whole-graph analysis rather than targeted traversal.

questions.question: Dataflow engines and graph processing both involve graphs. Why is conflating the two a mistake?

options.text: A dataflow engine's graph is a DAG of operators, whereas graph processing analyses graph-structured data
They really are the same thing: a dataflow DAG is just one way of drawing a graph algorithm out
Graph processing needs a cyclic operator graph, which no dataflow engine is able to express at all
Dataflow DAGs cannot express iterative algorithms, so graph algorithms must fall back on MapReduce

questions.explanation: Graph-shaped topology versus graph-shaped data.

questions.question: How are many graph algorithms expressed, and what is the worked example?

options.text: By traversing one edge at a time, repeatedly
By a single pass over all edges; the example is PageRank
By sorting vertices by degree; the example is clustering
By recursive SQL; the example is a join

questions.explanation: Repeat-until-converged is the shape, and transitive closure is the name of the example.

questions.question: Why does 'repeating until done' break plain MapReduce, and what is the workaround?

options.text: Repeating until done fits MapReduce badly, as it is not iterative
MapReduce supports iteration natively, so no workaround is needed
The reducer loops internally until convergence
The graph must be processed on a single machine

questions.explanation: This works, but implementing it with MapReduce is often very inefficient, because MapReduce does not account for the iterative nature of the algorithm: it will always read the entire input dataset and produce a completely new output dataset, even if only a small part of the graph has changed compared to the last iteration.

questions.question: Name the model that fixes this, its alternative name, and its implementations.

options.text: The bulk synchronous parallel model, implemented by Pregel
The MapReduce iteration model, implemented in Oozie
The dataflow model, implemented in Spark and Flink only
The actor model, implemented in Akka

questions.explanation: BSP and Pregel are two names for the same model.

questions.question: Describe Pregel's message-passing model and its crucial difference from MapReduce.

options.text: A vertex sends messages along its edges to other vertices
Pregel is stateless like MapReduce, but sends messages along edges
Pregel processes all vertices every iteration regardless of activity
Pregel eliminates message passing in favour of shared memory

questions.explanation: Persistent vertex state means work is proportional to activity, not graph size.

questions.question: How does Pregel differ from the actor model? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Vertex state and messages between vertices are fault-tolerant and durable, and communication is guaranteed
Communication proceeds in fixed rounds: at every iteration the framework delivers all messages sent in the previous iteration, whereas actors normally have no such timing guarantee
Pregel vertices are unable to send messages at all, which is unlike an actor
Pregel vertices carry no state between iterations, which is unlike an actor

questions.explanation: Durability and round-based delivery are the two differences. The fact that vertices can only communicate by message passing, not by querying each other directly, helps improve the performance of Pregel jobs, since messages can be batched and there is less waiting for communication. The only waiting is between iterations: since the model guarantees that all messages sent in one iteration are delivered in the next, the prior iteration must completely finish and all of its messages must be copied over the network before the next one can start. Even though the underlying network may drop, duplicate or arbitrarily delay messages, Pregel implementations guarantee that messages are processed exactly once at their destination vertex in the following iteration.

questions.question: How does Pregel achieve fault tolerance?

options.text: By checkpointing all vertex state at the end of an iteration
By replicating all vertex state synchronously to three machines
By recomputing from the original input on every failure with no checkpoints
It does not tolerate faults

questions.explanation: Checkpoints for the simple case, determinism plus message logs for selective recovery.

questions.question: What does a vertex know about its physical placement, and how are graphs partitioned in practice?

options.text: It addresses messages by vertex, not by machine
A vertex must specify the target machine when sending messages
The framework always finds the optimal partitioning
Graphs cannot be partitioned in Pregel

questions.explanation: Thinking like a vertex, with arbitrary partitioning in practice.

questions.question: Given the communication overhead, when should you not use a distributed graph algorithm?

options.text: Heavy cross-machine communication and large intermediate state
Always use a distributed algorithm; single machines are never competitive
Never use a distributed algorithm; graphs always fit on one machine
Use distributed algorithms only for graphs smaller than memory

questions.explanation: The same lesson as the single-machine awk/sort pipeline beating a Hadoop cluster.

questions.question: At what scale is the physical problem considered solved, and where did attention turn next?

options.text: Petabytes on clusters of over 10,000 machines
Clusters of 100 machines and terabytes; attention turned to hardware
Clusters of 1,000 machines; attention turned to security
Clusters of 100,000 machines; attention turned to networking

questions.explanation: Compare against the earlier figure: HDFS deployments on tens of thousands of machines with hundreds of petabytes.

questions.question: Why did the high-level languages win twice?

options.text: Because writing MapReduce jobs by hand is laborious
Because they were faster than raw MapReduce and required no rewrite for SQL
Because they supported streaming from the start
Because they eliminated the need for a cluster

questions.explanation: Less code first, then engine portability for free. These dataflow APIs generally use relational-style building blocks to express a computation: joining datasets on the value of some field, grouping tuples by key, filtering by some condition, and aggregating tuples by counting, summing or other functions — implemented internally using the various join and grouping algorithms discussed in the chapter.

questions.question: Beyond less code, what advantage do high-level interfaces bring?

options.text: Interactive incremental development in a shell
They eliminate the need for a cluster
They guarantee exactly-once semantics
They provide low-latency query responses

questions.explanation: Interactivity plus machine-level efficiency.

questions.question: What does a cost-based optimizer do for joins?

options.text: Because declared joins let the optimizer choose the algorithm
It rewrites the user-defined functions for greater speed
It chooses only the number of reducers to allocate
Cost-based optimization is absent from every batch processing framework

questions.explanation: Declarative specification is what makes automatic algorithm selection possible.

questions.question: How do MapReduce and its successors differ from SQL's fully declarative model, and what does that buy?

options.text: Around callbacks, not around declarative queries
They are fully declarative and cannot run arbitrary code
They use a restricted expression language with no callbacks
They differ only in syntax

questions.explanation: The freedom to easily run arbitrary code is what has long distinguished batch processing systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases. Although databases have facilities for writing user-defined functions, they are often cumbersome to use and not well integrated with the package managers and dependency management systems that are widely used in most programming languages — such as Maven for Java, npm for JavaScript and Rubygems for Ruby.

questions.question: Why does even a trivial filter benefit from being declared, and what optimizations does that unlock? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Because if a callback function contains only a simple filtering condition, or it just selects some fields from a record, then there is significant CPU overhead in calling the function on every record

Columnar reads: if such simple filtering and mapping operations are expressed in a declarative way, the query optimizer can take advantage of column-oriented storage layouts and read only the required columns from disk
Vectorized execution: Hive, Spark DataFrames and Impala use vectorized execution, iterating over data in a tight inner loop that is friendly to CPU caches and avoiding function calls
Code generation is deliberately avoided in these engines, since interpreting the callback directly turns out to be faster

questions.explanation: Both do generate code: Spark emits JVM bytecode and Impala uses LLVM to produce native code for the inner loops. By incorporating declarative aspects in their high-level APIs, and having query optimizers that can take advantage of them during execution, batch processing frameworks begin to look more like MPP databases and can achieve comparable performance — while by retaining the extensibility of being able to run arbitrary code and read data in arbitrary formats, they keep their flexibility advantage. As batch processing systems gain built-in functionality and high-level declarative operators, and as MPP databases become more programmable and flexible, the two are beginning to look more alike: in the end, they are all just systems for storing and processing data.

questions.question: Why is extensibility not enough on its own, and which reusable domain implementations exist?

options.text: Because standard processing patterns keep recurring
Extensibility is sufficient; no reusable libraries exist
Only Mahout exists, for machine learning
Reusable libraries exist only inside MPP databases

questions.explanation: Three domains with named, reusable implementations.

questions.question: Which design principles did MapReduce and the dataflow engines inherit from Unix?

options.text: Immutable inputs, output as another program's input, and composition
That programs should be monolithic, typed and interactive
That data should be modeled up front and validated on write
That outputs should be mutable and reused in place

questions.explanation: Note the parenthetical 'as yet unknown' — the program consuming your output may not exist yet.

questions.question: Give the uniform interface at each layer.

options.text: Files and pipes in Unix; a distributed filesystem in MapReduce
Unix uses pipes only; MapReduce uses pipes; dataflow engines use files
All three use the same distributed filesystem
Dataflow engines have no uniform interface

questions.explanation: Pipes in the middle, files at the edges.

questions.question: What are the two main problems distributed batch processing frameworks must solve, and how does each system solve them?

options.text: Partitioning, and fault tolerance
Replication and compression, solved identically by both
Scheduling and monitoring, solved by YARN in both cases
Encoding and serialization, solved by Avro in both cases

questions.explanation: Partitioning and fault tolerance, with opposite materialization trade-offs.

questions.question: Describe the three join algorithms available to a batch processor. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Sort-merge joins: each of the inputs being joined goes through a mapper that extracts the join key; by partitioning, sorting and merging, all the records with the same key end up going to the same call of the reducer, which can then output the joined records

Broadcast hash joins: one of the two join inputs is small, so it is not partitioned and can be entirely loaded into a hash table — thus you start a mapper for each partition of the large join input, load the hash table for the small input into each mapper, and then scan over the large input one record at a time, querying the hash table for each record

Partitioned hash joins: if the two join inputs are partitioned in the same way, using the same key, same hash function and same number of partitions, then the hash table approach can be used independently for each partition
These join algorithms are specific to MapReduce and have no real counterpart inside an MPP database

questions.explanation: Most of them are also used in MPP databases, which is part of why the chapter says MapReduce reinvented well-established ground. Three algorithms, useful beyond joining as a model of partitioned computation.

questions.question: State the restriction imposed on callback functions and what it buys.

options.text: Callback functions with hidden framework-managed state
Callbacks may be stateful and have side effects, which the framework tracks
The restriction buys only performance, not fault tolerance
Callbacks may do anything at all, since the framework imposes no restriction

questions.explanation: Statelessness and no side effects are what make transparent retry safe.

questions.question: What is the defining property of a batch processing job?

options.text: That it reads input and produces output without modifying the input
That it achieves the lowest possible latency for each individual record
That it keeps both its input and its output inside HDFS specifically
That it always takes the shape of one map step and one reduce step

questions.explanation: Bounded input is what makes completion meaningful — and losing it is what makes stream processing different.
